tasks.locator: Results › LTFU questionnaire results for 19 PTSD subjects › Degree of benefit, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Results › Questions about illicit drug use during LTFU period
tasks.extracted: On the investigators' own follow-up questionnaire, all 19 MDMA-treated participants reported some benefit and none reported harm from taking part; cannabis use by 8 (once to occasionally) and psilocybin mushrooms by 1, all of whom reported use before enrolment; 1 participant reported using ecstasy once, in an attempt at a therapeutic setting, and found it unsatisfactory.

tasks.locator: Methods and materials › Study design, 2nd paragraph; Footnotes › Conflict of interest
tasks.extracted: The follow-up CAPS was administered in person or by phone by the same independent rater as in the original trial; the sponsor paid this rater, who is the second author, and played a role in the study design, data analysis and writing.

tasks.locator: Corrected Table 3; Summary of corrections made › Open-label endpoints, 1st paragraph (revised text)
tasks.extracted: Corrected open-label analysis of the four pooled trials (N = 58): CAPS-IV least-squares means 88.22 at baseline, 42.46 at treatment exit and 35.28 at 12-month follow-up; treatment exit to 12 months −7.18 (SE 2.60), p = .008.

tasks.locator: Results › Open-Label Endpoints: Treatment Exit and Long-Term Follow-Up, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 note; Method › Measures › PTSD Symptoms, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: After the blinded endpoint, all participants received full-dose MDMA in open-label sessions; groups were pooled for treatment exit and the 12-month follow-up, which took place after the final open-label session, so these comparisons are within-person and uncontrolled. CAPS-IV total severity scores range from 0 to 136.

tasks.locator: Notice, 2nd to 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Expression of concern (3 December 2024): an ethical violation by a pair of therapists who treated 4 of the 6 MP-4 participants caused a protocol deviation; the authors had not told the journal at submission in December 2019, although the violation was publicly announced in May 2019; the data of those therapists are removed by correction; the journal judged the non-disclosure improper and its investigation of human-subjects ethics inconclusive.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Jerome 2020 row)
tasks.extracted: Across the studies reviewed to October 2023, conclusions were possible only for acute and short-term side effects, because insufficient data were available on longer-term risks beyond active treatment; the one included study that formally assessed long-term follow-up outcomes was the pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials by Jerome et al. (2020), which the PMC reference list now marks as retracted.

tasks.locator: Conclusion, 7th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Among the review's research priorities: longer follow-ups in clinical trials, because short-term outcomes, positive and negative, often change in the weeks and months after a typical trial ends.

tasks.locator: Results › Blinded Endpoint, 1st paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Original analysis, superseded by the correction: PSQI change −3.53 (SD 5.03) in the active group against +0.56 (3.05) in the control group (n = 16; active n printed as 46 in Table 2 and 47 elsewhere), p = .003, Hedges' g 0.88 with a printed 95% CI of −0.27 to 2.03 that does not fit g; a drop of 3 points or more in 53.2% against 12.5% (N = 61).

tasks.locator: Summary of corrections made › Blinded endpoint, 1st paragraph (revised text); corrected Table 2
tasks.extracted: Corrected blinded endpoint: PSQI change −3.51 (SD 5.08) in the active group (n = 44) against +0.50 (3.25) in the control group (n = 14), p = .008, Hedges' g 0.85 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.47); CAPS-IV −34.93 against −11.07, g 0.96 (0.33 to 1.59).

tasks.locator: Corrected Table 2, note b
tasks.extracted: PSQI fell by 3 points or more in 24 active participants (53.3%, of 45) and 2 controls (14.3%, of 14), p = .008; the footnote's counts and denominators do not fully agree (19 active without such a drop, n = 44 in the table).

tasks.locator: Corrected Table 3
tasks.extracted: Open-label (N = 58): PSQI least-squares means 12.59 at baseline, 8.18 at treatment exit, 7.09 at 12 months; change from exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029.

tasks.locator: Description and explanation for this correction; Summary of corrections made › In the abstract
tasks.extracted: The four MP-4 participants treated by the pair of therapists were removed; sample 63 to 59 (active 47 to 45, control 16 to 14); the removed participants were the only ones in the control group given no MDMA, so the control group now consists only of low-dose MDMA and the placebo label is dropped.

tasks.locator: Notice, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors had not notified the journal of the ethical violation at submission (December 2019), although it had been publicly announced in May 2019; the journal judged this improper and issued the expression of concern; its investigation of human-subjects ethics was inconclusive.

tasks.locator: Method › Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Open Practices Statement
tasks.extracted: Doses pooled into control and active groups by the protocols' designations and by inspection of post-treatment CAPS-IV scores (citing the since-retracted pooled analysis by Mithoefer et al., 2019); independent-samples t tests; no power analysis; the analyses were not formally preregistered.

tasks.locator: Method › Measures › Sleep Quality, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Sleep quality was measured with the self-report PSQI (global score 0 to 21; a cut-off of 5 separates good from poor sleepers); the authors list the small, mostly White sample and self-reported outcomes as limitations; the paper reports no assessment of whether participants could tell their dose.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Entactogens (MDMA) › Anxiety and Depression; Summary of findings 2
tasks.extracted: One trial (Wolfson 2020; 18 participants): STAI-T mean difference −14.70 (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05) and STAI-S −16.10 (−33.03 to 0.83), both on 20 to 80 scales; BDI-II −6.30 (−16.93 to 4.33) on a 0 to 63 scale; 1 month after the second session; very low certainty, downgraded once for risk of bias and twice for imprecision.

tasks.locator: Results › Description of studies › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Ongoing studies
tasks.extracted: Searched on 30 March 2024: of six randomized trials in people with life-threatening diseases, one evaluated MDMA (18 randomized and analysed); seven ongoing trials, of psilocybin, LSD and ketamine, none of MDMA.

tasks.locator: Results › MDMA, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Other disorders rows)
tasks.extracted: Besides PTSD, randomized trials of MDMA in end-of-life anxiety (Wolfson 2020, 13 MDMA and 5 placebo), social anxiety in adults with autism (Danforth 2018, 12) and tinnitus (Searchfield 2020, 13), and an open-label study in alcohol use disorder (Sessa 2019, 2021; 14).

tasks.locator: Table 1
tasks.extracted: Of 13 studies to October 2023, the only randomized trial outside PTSD was in autistic adults with social anxiety (12); others outside PTSD were an open-label alcohol use disorder study (14) and a Swiss case series of various treatment-resistant disorders; the uncontrolled couples study (6 couples) enrolled dyads with one partner with PTSD.

tasks.locator: Fig. 2, upper and middle panels (values printed in the figure image); Results › Network meta-analysis, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: High-dose MDMA against the placebo arms of psychedelic trials 5.32 HAMD-17 points (95% CrI 2.26 to 8.32); against the placebo arms of escitalopram trials 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78), the two parts of the network being joined only by one head-to-head psilocybin-escitalopram trial; participants in the MDMA trials were predominantly diagnosed with PTSD, those in the escitalopram trials with major depressive disorder.

tasks.locator: Minimal research quality standards imposed in this review, 3rd paragraph; Safety and Effectiveness of Psychedelic Drugs › MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 1st paragraph; Summary of Effectiveness Evidence for Psychedelic Medicines, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Standard: randomized trials in diagnosed disorders with more than 15 participants per condition; for MDMA only the two phase 3 PTSD trials, run by a consortium funded by MAPS, are discussed; because of absent successful blinding and likely expectancy effects, MDMA for PTSD is a positive signal that should not be taken as definitive without replication in methodologically stronger studies.

tasks.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st paragraph; Results › Effects of interventions, 2nd paragraph; Characteristics of included studies › Wolfson 2020 (risk-of-bias table)
tasks.extracted: Blinding could not be achieved in any included trial; in the MDMA trial more than 80% of investigators and participants guessed the assignment correctly and most outcomes were self-reported; all outcomes after more than 3 months were measured after crossover, without a comparison group.

tasks.locator: Abstract; Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: From the relatively poor data in the literature and information given personally to the author, a few dozen therapists, most in California and elsewhere on the West Coast, used MDMA in psychotherapy between 1977 (title and abstract) or 1978 (Discussion) and 1985, when it was neither an FDA-approved drug nor a controlled substance; a physician could use it legally if self-synthesized, with informed consent and a peer-reviewed protocol.

tasks.locator: George Greer's work with MDMA in psychotherapy, 1st and 5th paragraphs; Leo Zeff—The Secret Chief, 2nd paragraph; Rick Ingrasci: MDMA in couples and patients with life-threatening illnesses, 1st paragraph; A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Greer, a psychiatrist, and Tolbert, a psychiatric nurse, treated more than 80 patients from 1980 to 1985; their published follow-up of 29 patients found no serious side effects or negative after-effects and 23 with positive changes lasting from 1 week to 2 years; Zeff gave MDMA to about 4000 people over 12 years (from a memoir); Ingrasci treated 100 patients in about 150 sessions, one-third with couples; Harlow treated more than 200 clients before 1985.

tasks.locator: A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Kueny's 1980 study, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: A 1984 exploratory survey of 16 therapists for ARUPA: 15 judged MDMA valuable in augmenting psychotherapy and all claimed complications were negligible; it was used as evidence at the hearings; an unpublished 1980 study gave one MDMA session to each of nine people.

tasks.locator: Physical abuse in MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Two therapists, Rick Ingrasci and Francesco DiLeo, initiated intimate body contact, sexual touch and intercourse with patients during MDMA sessions; both were sued and lost their licences; a Maryland appeals court (1991) upheld damages to DiLeo's patient, later diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety.

tasks.locator: Therapists opposed to the scheduling of MDMA in 1985, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th, 6th and 8th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The DEA recommended Schedule I on 27 July 1984; at the 1985 hearings its administrative law judge concluded that MDMA did not have to be placed in Schedule I; the DEA overruled the judge's decision; the WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, which scheduled MDMA internationally in late 1985, found the therapeutic reports intriguing but methodologically inadequate and urged research; five applications to study MDMA submitted from 1986 to 1988 were placed on clinical hold; after the FDA rejected a patient study and recommended a study in healthy volunteers, the first FDA-approved MDMA study in humans began in 1992.
